claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was about ten feet long/tall
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man"

claims.claim: The giant was dug up behind a barn
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: The discovery took place in Cardiff, New York on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: The photograph of the giant is by Bain News Service, 1910, public domain
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher
Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: A lithograph of the giant listing its measurements exists
claims.quote: ITS DIMENSIONS ARE

claims.claim: Whole length of the figure: 10 feet 4½ inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: The giant weighed about 2,990 pounds
claims.quote: it weighed 2,990 pounds (1,360 kg)

claims.claim: The lithograph is titled "The Onondaga Giant" and is credited to Popular Graphic Arts, public domain
claims.quote: Archive title: File:The Onondaga giant LCCN2003666806.jpg

claims.claim: The block was taken from a gypsum quarry in Iowa
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: George Hull's men cut the block at Fort Dodge, having been told it was for a Lincoln monument
claims.quote: Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: The block was shipped to Chicago and carved there
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter. Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: The quarry image is "View in Cardiff Glen", Iowa, 1873, public domain
claims.quote:
Description: View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa.
Date: 1873

claims.claim: The souvenir card names the perpetrators of the imposture
claims.quote: The perpetrators of the imposture are well remembered by old residents of Fort Dodge. Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: The card text says the giant was carved in Chicago, buried in a barn lot in New York, and subsequently discovered
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name, where it was buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered".

claims.claim: The card was printed in 1873
claims.quote: Date: 1873

claims.claim: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores.

claims.claim: Sulphuric acid was used to deepen the colour
claims.quote: The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: Marsh observed fresh tool marks on the soluble gypsum and called it a humbug
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: It is unclear whether the stonecutter knew what he was carving
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: Hull confessed in December 1869 (10 December 1869)
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: Both giants were ruled fakes in court in February 1870
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: In 1868 George Hull, a New York tobacconist, lost a debate at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Hull was a New York tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull was angered by people's credulity and set out to prove how easily they could be fooled
claims.quote: Angered by his defeat and the credulity of people, Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant.

claims.claim: Two sculptors carved a figure modelled on Hull himself
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant. ... The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: Quilts were hung to muffle the sound of carving
claims.quote: putting up quilts to lessen the sound of carving

claims.claim: Hull removed the hair after learning from a geologist that hair does not petrify
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Sand and water were used on the surface
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water

claims.claim: The hoax cost $2,600
claims.quote: By then, he had spent US$2,600 (equivalent to $63,000 in 2025) for the hoax.

claims.claim: The giant was buried behind the barn of Hull's cousin William Newell
claims.quote: During November 1868, Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell.

claims.claim: It was "found" by well-diggers on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing
claims.quote: a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people came per day
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: Andrew D. White of Cornell noted there was no reason to dig a well in that spot
claims.quote: Andrew D. White, the first president of Cornell University, made a close inspection of the Cardiff Giant. He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Othniel Marsh was a Yale paleontologist
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue

claims.claim: Edward Burkhardt was the Chicago stonecutter
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: A Michigan arcade owner claims its Cardiff Giant is Barnum's copy, which is the owner's claim rather than proven provenance
claims.quote: The owner of Marvin's Marvelous Mechanical Museum, a coin-operated game arcade and museum of oddities in Farmington Hills, Michigan, has said that the copy displayed there is Barnum's.

claims.claim: Barnum's copy was unauthorised
claims.quote: Both it and an unauthorized copy made by P. T. Barnum are still being displayed.
